claim: Atoh1-null mice die at birth from respiratory failure.
source: Atoh1-null mice die at birth from respiratory failure, but the precise cause has remained elusive.
evidence: This is a well-established finding cited in the abstract and supported by references to prior work (Ben-Arie et al., 1997; Rose et al., 2009b; Tupal et al., 2014).

claim: Loss of Atoh1 from the retrotrapezoid nucleus (RTN) has produced at most 50% neonatal lethality.
source: Loss of Atoh1 from various components of the respiratory circuitry (e.g. the retrotrapezoid nucleus (RTN)) has so far produced at most 50% neonatal lethality.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citation to Huang et al., 2012 in the introduction.

claim: Parabrachial complex neurons derived from the rostral rhombic lip (rRL) are activated during respiratory chemochallenges.
source: we examined parabrachial complex neurons derived from the rostral rhombic lip (rRL) and found that they are activated during respiratory chemochallenges.
evidence: This is directly stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Atoh1-deletion from the rRL does not affect survival.
source: Atoh1-deletion from the rRL does not affect survival, but causes apneas and respiratory depression during hypoxia, likely due to loss of projections to the preBötzinger Complex and RTN.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by survival data in Figure 1D showing Mendelian ratios.

claim: Atoh1-deletion from the rRL causes apneas during hypoxia.
source: Atoh1-deletion from the rRL does not affect survival, but causes apneas and respiratory depression during hypoxia, likely due to loss of projections to the preBötzinger Complex and RTN.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by plethysmography data in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: Atoh1-deletion from the rRL causes respiratory depression during hypoxia.
source: Atoh1-deletion from the rRL does not affect survival, but causes apneas and respiratory depression during hypoxia, likely due to loss of projections to the preBötzinger Complex and RTN.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by plethysmography data showing decreased respiratory frequency and minute ventilation during hypoxia in Figure 3.

claim: Loss of projections to the preBötzinger Complex and RTN likely causes the respiratory phenotypes in Atoh1::En1-CKO mice.
source: Atoh1-deletion from the rRL does not affect survival, but causes apneas and respiratory depression during hypoxia, likely due to loss of projections to the preBötzinger Complex and RTN.
evidence: This is stated as a likely explanation in the abstract and supported by anatomical tracing data in Figure 5.

claim: Atoh1 promotes the development of neural circuits governing hypoxic chemoresponses.
source: Atoh1 thus promotes the development of the neural circuits governing hypoxic (rRL) and hypercapnic (RTN) chemoresponses, and combined loss of Atoh1 from these regions causes fully penetrant neonatal lethality.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data showing impaired hypoxic responses in Atoh1::En1-CKO mice (Figures 3 and 4).

claim: Atoh1 promotes the development of neural circuits governing hypercapnic chemoresponses.
source: Atoh1 thus promotes the development of the neural circuits governing hypoxic (rRL) and hypercapnic (RTN) chemoresponses, and combined loss of Atoh1 from these regions causes fully penetrant neonatal lethality.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by prior work on RTN (Huang et al., 2012) and data in Figure 3 showing attenuated hypercapnic responses.

claim: Combined loss of Atoh1 from the rRL and RTN causes fully penetrant neonatal lethality.
source: Atoh1 thus promotes the development of the neural circuits governing hypoxic (rRL) and hypercapnic (RTN) chemoresponses, and combined loss of Atoh1 from these regions causes fully penetrant neonatal lethality.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by survival data in Figure 7—figure supplement 1 showing 0% survival of Atoh1-dCKO mice.

claim: Modulating respiratory rhythms in response to chemosensory information is important during early postnatal life.
source: This work underscores the importance of modulating respiratory rhythms in response to chemosensory information during early postnatal life.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the abstract and supported by the overall findings of the study.

claim: Circuits giving rise to vital functions such as respiration must be functional from birth without trial and error learning.
source: Yet circuits giving rise to vital functions, such as respiration, have no time for such trial and error: the animal must be able to maintain its own O2/CO2 homeostasis from the moment it is born.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a general principle about respiratory circuit development.

claim: The ability to maintain O2/CO2 homeostasis from birth likely arises from a detailed genetic blueprint in the hindbrain respiratory circuit.
source: This ability likely arises from a detailed genetic blueprint in the hindbrain respiratory circuit.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as an inference about how respiratory circuits develop.

claim: Mapping the expression domains of key transcription factors in the developing hindbrain reveals a checkerboard pattern.
source: Indeed, mapping the expression domains of key transcription factors in the developing hindbrain reveals a checkerboard pattern, with rostro-caudal and dorso-ventral stripes crisscrossing the entire region (Gray, 2008, 2013; Pagliardini et al., 2008; Pasqualetti et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by multiple citations.

claim: Mice lacking Atoh1 generate some respiratory movements despite dying at birth.
source: For example, mice lacking the transcription factor Atonal homolog 1 (Atoh1) die at birth of respiratory failure even though they generate some respiratory movements (Ben-Arie et al., 1997; Rose et al., 2009b; Tupal et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Atoh1 is expressed in the developing hindbrain along the entire rostro-caudal rhombic lip.
source: Atoh1 is expressed in the developing hindbrain along the entire rostro-caudal rhombic lip, where it promotes the development of several nuclei involved in respiratory control (Gray, 2013; Rose et al., 2009a, 2009b; Wang et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations and Figure 1A.

claim: Atoh1 promotes the development of several nuclei involved in respiratory control.
source: Atoh1 is expressed in the developing hindbrain along the entire rostro-caudal rhombic lip, where it promotes the development of several nuclei involved in respiratory control (Gray, 2013; Rose et al., 2009a, 2009b; Wang et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: Atoh1 is expressed in postmitotic neurons of the intertrigeminal region (ITR).
source: Atoh1 is also expressed in postmitotic neurons of two paramotor nuclei: the intertrigeminal region (ITR) and the retrotrapezoid nucleus (RTN) (Figure 1A and B) (Huang et al., 2012; Rose et al., 2009b).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations and Figure 1A and B.

claim: Atoh1 is expressed in postmitotic neurons of the retrotrapezoid nucleus (RTN).
source: Atoh1 is also expressed in postmitotic neurons of two paramotor nuclei: the intertrigeminal region (ITR) and the retrotrapezoid nucleus (RTN) (Figure 1A and B) (Huang et al., 2012; Rose et al., 2009b).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations and Figure 1A and B.

claim: The chemosensitive RTN sends excitatory projections to the preBötzinger complex (preBötC).
source: The chemosensitive RTN sends excitatory projections to the preBötzinger complex (preBötC), which generates inspiratory rhythms (Guyenet and Bayliss, 2015; Guyenet et al., 2010; Kumar et al., 2015; Onimaru and Homma, 2003).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by multiple citations.

claim: The preBötzinger complex (preBötC) generates inspiratory rhythms.
source: The chemosensitive RTN sends excitatory projections to the preBötzinger complex (preBötC), which generates inspiratory rhythms (Guyenet and Bayliss, 2015; Guyenet et al., 2010; Kumar et al., 2015; Onimaru and Homma, 2003).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by multiple citations.

claim: Atoh1 loss from the RTN impairs respiratory responses to hypercapnia.
source: Atoh1 loss from the RTN impairs respiratory responses to hypercapnia, but, rather remarkably, causes only partial neonatal lethality (Huang et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citation to Huang et al., 2012.

claim: Atoh1 loss from the RTN causes only partial neonatal lethality.
source: Atoh1 loss from the RTN impairs respiratory responses to hypercapnia, but, rather remarkably, causes only partial neonatal lethality (Huang et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citation to Huang et al., 2012.

claim: Atoh1-lineage PBC neurons do not express cFos after exposure to room air.
source: We found tdTomato+, cFos+ double-positive cells in the medial and lateral parabrachial region as well as in the Kölliker Fuse after exposure to either hypoxia or hypercapnia, but not room air (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1C where room air exposure does not result in cFos expression.

claim: Atoh1-lineage PBC neurons are activated by changes in O2 and CO2.
source: This confirms that Atoh1-lineage PBC neurons are activated by changes in O2 and CO2 and might play a role in respiratory function.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on the cFos expression data in Figure 1C.

claim: Atoh1-lineage PBC neurons might play a role in respiratory function.
source: This confirms that Atoh1-lineage PBC neurons are activated by changes in O2 and CO2 and might play a role in respiratory function.
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis based on the cFos expression data.

claim: Atoh1-null mice lose the substance P receptor NK1R in the PBC region.
source: Previous studies showed that Atoh1-null mice lose the substance P receptor NK1R in the PBC region (Rose et al., 2009b).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by citation to Rose et al., 2009b.

claim: All NK1R-expressing PBC neurons are Atoh1-lineage neurons.
source: We found that indeed all NK1R-expressing PBC neurons were Atoh1-lineage neurons (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: All counted Atoh1-lineage neurons in the lateral PBC express CGRP.
source: We found that all counted Atoh1-lineage neurons in the lateral PBC expressed CGRP and that some expressed PACAP (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Some Atoh1-lineage neurons in the lateral PBC express PACAP.
source: We found that all counted Atoh1-lineage neurons in the lateral PBC expressed CGRP and that some expressed PACAP (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Atoh1::En1-CKO mice are born in Mendelian ratios.
source: Atoh1Flox/LacZ;En1Cre/+ mice (hereafter Atoh1::En1-CKO) were born in Mendelian ratios (25/97 surviving pups, Figure 1D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by survival data in Figure 1D.

claim: Atoh1::En1-CKO mice lost all Atoh1-expressing neurons from the rRL at E14.5.
source: We stained E14.5 embryos with X-gal and confirmed that Atoh1::En1-CKO lost all Atoh1-expressing neurons from the rRL, while leaving other Atoh1-lineage neurons intact (Figure 1E and F).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by X-gal staining data in Figure 1E and F.

claim: Atoh1::En1-CKO mice retain other Atoh1-lineage neurons outside the rRL at E14.5.
source: We stained E14.5 embryos with X-gal and confirmed that Atoh1::En1-CKO lost all Atoh1-expressing neurons from the rRL, while leaving other Atoh1-lineage neurons intact (Figure 1E and F).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by X-gal staining data in Figure 1E and F.

claim: Conditional deletion of Atoh1 in Atoh1::En1-CKO mice results in loss of NK1R-expressing PBC neurons at P21.
source: Anatomical analysis of postnatal (P21) animals confirmed that this conditional deletion of Atoh1 resulted in loss of NK1R-expressing PBC neurons (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 1G.

claim: Atoh1::En1-CKO mice survive despite losing Atoh1-lineage PBC neurons.
source: Thus, despite losing these Atoh1-lineage PBC neurons, these animals survive, showing that Atoh1 expression in the rRL is not necessary for neonatal survival.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by survival data in Figure 1D.

claim: Atoh1 expression in the rRL is not necessary for neonatal survival.
source: Thus, despite losing these Atoh1-lineage PBC neurons, these animals survive, showing that Atoh1 expression in the rRL is not necessary for neonatal survival.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on the survival of Atoh1::En1-CKO mice.

claim: Atoh1::En1-CKO mice develop severe ataxia in the second to third week after birth.
source: Atoh1::En1-CKO mice developed severe ataxia, dystonia and tremor in the second to third week after birth and died shortly after weaning (P22-25), probably because the motor phenotypes impair their ability to get proper amounts of food and water.
evidence: This is stated in the text as an observation of the phenotype.

claim: Atoh1::En1-CKO mice develop dystonia in the second to third week after birth.
source: Atoh1::En1-CKO mice developed severe ataxia, dystonia and tremor in the second to third week after birth and died shortly after weaning (P22-25), probably because the motor phenotypes impair their ability to get proper amounts of food and water.
evidence: This is stated in the text as an observation of the phenotype.

claim: Atoh1::En1-CKO mice develop tremor in the second to third week after birth.
source: Atoh1::En1-CKO mice developed severe ataxia, dystonia and tremor in the second to third week after birth and died shortly after weaning (P22-25), probably because the motor phenotypes impair their ability to get proper amounts of food and water.
evidence: This is stated in the text as an observation of the phenotype.

claim: Atoh1::En1-CKO mice die shortly after weaning (P22-25).
source: Atoh1::En1-CKO mice developed severe ataxia, dystonia and tremor in the second to third week after birth and died shortly after weaning (P22-25), probably because the motor phenotypes impair their ability to get proper amounts of food and water.
evidence: This is stated in the text as an observation.

claim: The motor phenotypes in Atoh1::En1-CKO mice probably impair their ability to get proper amounts of food and water.
source: Atoh1::En1-CKO mice developed severe ataxia, dystonia and tremor in the second to third week after birth and died shortly after weaning (P22-25), probably because the motor phenotypes impair their ability to get proper amounts of food and water.
evidence: This is stated as a probable explanation for the post-weaning death.

claim: The motor phenotypes in Atoh1::En1-CKO mice are likely the result of loss of Atoh1-lineage cerebellar neurons including glutamatergic deep cerebellar nuclei and cerebellar granule cells.
source: These phenotypes were likely the result of loss of Atoh1-lineage cerebellar neurons including glutamatergic deep cerebellar nuclei and cerebellar granule cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A) (Ben-Arie et al., 1997; Wurst et al., 1994).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by anatomical data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A and citations.

claim: Atoh1-lineage cerebellar neurons are not activated during respiratory chemochallenges.
source: Unlike Atoh1-lineage PBC neurons, however, these Atoh1-lineage cerebellar neurons are not activated during respiratory chemochallenges and are thus less likely to be important for respiratory chemoresponses (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B and C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by cFos expression data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B and C.

claim: Atoh1-lineage cerebellar neurons are less likely to be important for respiratory chemoresponses.
source: Unlike Atoh1-lineage PBC neurons, however, these Atoh1-lineage cerebellar neurons are not activated during respiratory chemochallenges and are thus less likely to be important for respiratory chemoresponses (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B and C).
evidence: This is stated as an inference based on the lack of cFos activation.

claim: Atoh1::En1-CKO mice have a greater number of sigh-induced apneas than control littermates in room air at P21.
source: In room air, Atoh1::En1-CKO mice had a greater number of sigh-induced and spontaneous apneas, sighs, and irregular respiratory rhythms than their control littermates (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by plethysmography data in Figure 2B.

claim: Atoh1::En1-CKO mice have a greater number of spontaneous apneas than control littermates in room air at P21.
source: In room air, Atoh1::En1-CKO mice had a greater number of sigh-induced and spontaneous apneas, sighs, and irregular respiratory rhythms than their control littermates (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by plethysmography data in Figure 2B.

claim: Atoh1::En1-CKO mice have a greater number of sighs than control littermates in room air at P21.
source: In room air, Atoh1::En1-CKO mice had a greater number of sigh-induced and spontaneous apneas, sighs, and irregular respiratory rhythms than their control littermates (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by plethysmography data in Figure 2B.

claim: Atoh1::En1-CKO mice have more irregular respiratory rhythms than control littermates in room air at P21.
source: In room air, Atoh1::En1-CKO mice had a greater number of sigh-induced and spontaneous apneas, sighs, and irregular respiratory rhythms than their control littermates (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by plethysmography data in Figure 2B.

claim: Apneas, sighs, and rhythmic irregularity are hallmarks of immature respiration that can occur in some human infants.
source: Apneas, sighs, and rhythmic irregularity are hallmarks of immature respiration that can occur in some human infants (Abu-Shaweesh and Martin, 2008; Martin et al., 2004; Abu-Shaweesh, 2004).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by citations to clinical literature.

claim: Infants with apnea of prematurity (AOP) are treated with caffeine to stabilize their breathing rhythms.
source: When infants present with apnea of prematurity (AOP) in a clinical setting, they are treated with caffeine to stabilize their breathing rhythms (Aranda et al., 1977; Natarajan et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by citations to clinical literature.

claim: Caffeine treatment normalized apnea frequency in Atoh1::En1-CKO mice.
source: Caffeine treatment normalized apnea frequency and irregular breathing rhythms, but not sighs (Figure 2B), showing that caffeine is sufficient to stabilize irregular breathing rhythms in our mice similar to human infants.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by plethysmography data in Figure 2B.

claim: Caffeine treatment normalized irregular breathing rhythms in Atoh1::En1-CKO mice.
source: Caffeine treatment normalized apnea frequency and irregular breathing rhythms, but not sighs (Figure 2B), showing that caffeine is sufficient to stabilize irregular breathing rhythms in our mice similar to human infants.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by plethysmography data in Figure 2B.

claim: Caffeine treatment did not normalize sighs in Atoh1::En1-CKO mice.
source: Caffeine treatment normalized apnea frequency and irregular breathing rhythms, but not sighs (Figure 2B), showing that caffeine is sufficient to stabilize irregular breathing rhythms in our mice similar to human infants.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by plethysmography data in Figure 2B.

claim: Caffeine is sufficient to stabilize irregular breathing rhythms in Atoh1::En1-CKO mice similar to human infants.
source: Caffeine treatment normalized apnea frequency and irregular breathing rhythms, but not sighs (Figure 2B), showing that caffeine is sufficient to stabilize irregular breathing rhythms in our mice similar to human infants.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on the caffeine treatment data.

claim: Caffeine treatment significantly decreased minute ventilation in control mice.
source: Much to our surprise, this method of caffeine treatment also significantly decreased minute ventilation in control mice, as a result of both decreased tidal volume and breathing frequency (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by plethysmography data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Caffeine treatment decreased tidal volume in control mice.
source: Much to our surprise, this method of caffeine treatment also significantly decreased minute ventilation in control mice, as a result of both decreased tidal volume and breathing frequency (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by plethysmography data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Caffeine treatment decreased breathing frequency in control mice.
source: Much to our surprise, this method of caffeine treatment also significantly decreased minute ventilation in control mice, as a result of both decreased tidal volume and breathing frequency (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by plethysmography data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Atoh1::En1-CKO mice showed a decrease in tidal volume with caffeine treatment.
source: Although Atoh1::En1-CKO mice also showed a decrease in tidal volume, they seemingly compensated by increasing their rate of respiration, resulting in normal minute ventilation compared to control conditions.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by plethysmography data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Atoh1::En1-CKO mice compensated for decreased tidal volume by increasing their rate of respiration with caffeine treatment.
source: Although Atoh1::En1-CKO mice also showed a decrease in tidal volume, they seemingly compensated by increasing their rate of respiration, resulting in normal minute ventilation compared to control conditions.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by plethysmography data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Atoh1::En1-CKO mice had normal minute ventilation with caffeine treatment compared to control conditions.
source: Although Atoh1::En1-CKO mice also showed a decrease in tidal volume, they seemingly compensated by increasing their rate of respiration, resulting in normal minute ventilation compared to control conditions.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by plethysmography data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Control mice had a short initial increase in tidal volume during hypoxia.
source: Control mice had a short initial increase in tidal volume and breathing frequency that returned to baseline within several minutes of exposure to hypoxia (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by plethysmography data in Figure 3A.

claim: Control mice had a short initial increase in breathing frequency during hypoxia.
source: Control mice had a short initial increase in tidal volume and breathing frequency that returned to baseline within several minutes of exposure to hypoxia (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by plethysmography data in Figure 3B.

claim: Control mice showed a bimodal response in minute ventilation during hypoxia.
source: This resulted in a bimodal response in minute ventilation (Figure 3C), similar to what others have reported in juvenile mice (Haddad and Mellins, 1984; Waters and Gozal, 2003).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by plethysmography data in Figure 3C and citations.

claim: Atoh1::En1-CKO mice showed a brief initial increase in tidal volume during hypoxia.
source: Atoh1::En1-CKO mice also showed a brief initial increase in tidal volume (Figure 3A), but this was accompanied by a rapid, sustained decrease in respiratory rate that repressed minute ventilation during hypoxia (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by plethysmography data in Figure 3A.

claim: Atoh1::En1-CKO mice showed a rapid, sustained decrease in respiratory rate during hypoxia.
source: Atoh1::En1-CKO mice also showed a brief initial increase in tidal volume (Figure 3A), but this was accompanied by a rapid, sustained decrease in respiratory rate that repressed minute ventilation during hypoxia (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by plethysmography data in Figure 3B and D.

claim: Atoh1::En1-CKO mice showed repressed minute ventilation during hypoxia.
source: Atoh1::En1-CKO mice also showed a brief initial increase in tidal volume (Figure 3A), but this was accompanied by a rapid, sustained decrease in respiratory rate that repressed minute ventilation during hypoxia (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by plethysmography data in Figure 3D.

claim: Caffeine treatment in control mice prolonged the respiratory response to hypoxia by limiting respiratory depression.
source: Interestingly, while caffeine treatment in control mice did prolong the respiratory response to hypoxia by limiting respiratory depression during exposure to hypoxic gas (Figure 3C), it did not improve respiratory chemoresponses in Atoh1::En1-CKO mice (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by plethysmography data in Figure 3C.

claim: Caffeine treatment did not improve respiratory chemoresponses to hypoxia in Atoh1::En1-CKO mice.
source: Interestingly, while caffeine treatment in control mice did prolong the respiratory response to hypoxia by limiting respiratory depression during exposure to hypoxic gas (Figure 3C), it did not improve respiratory chemoresponses in Atoh1::En1-CKO mice (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by plethysmography data in Figure 3D.

claim: Respiratory depression in response to hypoxia resembles the suppression of fetal breathing movements during hypoxia in prenatal mammals.
source: Respiratory depression in response to hypoxia resembles the suppression of fetal breathing movements during hypoxia in prenatal mammals (Gluckman and Johnston, 1987; Haddad and Mellins, 1984; Abu-Shaweesh, 2004; Waters and Gozal, 2003), underscoring how loss of rRL neurons recapitulates many aspects of immature breathing control.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Loss of rRL neurons recapitulates many aspects of immature breathing control.
source: Respiratory depression in response to hypoxia resembles the suppression of fetal breathing movements during hypoxia in prenatal mammals (Gluckman and Johnston, 1987; Haddad and Mellins, 1984; Abu-Shaweesh, 2004; Waters and Gozal, 2003), underscoring how loss of rRL neurons recapitulates many aspects of immature breathing control.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on the observed phenotypes and citations.

claim: Control mice showed a rapid increase in tidal volume during hypercapnia.
source: We found that control littermates showed a rapid increase in tidal volume and breathing frequency during hypercapnia, whereas respiratory chemoresponses of Atoh1::En1-CKO mice were severely attenuated (Figure 3E and F).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by plethysmography data in Figure 3E.

claim: Control mice showed a rapid increase in breathing frequency during hypercapnia.
source: We found that control littermates showed a rapid increase in tidal volume and breathing frequency during hypercapnia, whereas respiratory chemoresponses of Atoh1::En1-CKO mice were severely attenuated (Figure 3E and F).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by plethysmography data in Figure 3F.

claim: Respiratory chemoresponses to hypercapnia of Atoh1::En1-CKO mice were severely attenuated.
source: We found that control littermates showed a rapid increase in tidal volume and breathing frequency during hypercapnia, whereas respiratory chemoresponses of Atoh1::En1-CKO mice were severely attenuated (Figure 3E and F).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by plethysmography data in Figure 3E and F.

claim: Caffeine treatment delayed the return to baseline minute ventilation in control mice during hypercapnia.
source: Caffeine treatment delayed the return to baseline minute ventilation in control mice, but did not improve the hypercapnic chemoresponses of Atoh1::En1-CKO littermates (Figure 3G and H).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by plethysmography data in Figure 3G.

claim: Caffeine treatment did not improve the hypercapnic chemoresponses of Atoh1::En1-CKO mice.
source: Caffeine treatment delayed the return to baseline minute ventilation in control mice, but did not improve the hypercapnic chemoresponses of Atoh1::En1-CKO littermates (Figure 3G and H).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by plethysmography data in Figure 3H.

claim: The mechanism by which caffeine rescues apneas, sighs, and irregular respiratory rhythms in Atoh1::En1-CKO mice cannot be through normalizing chemoresponses.
source: Thus, the mechanism by which caffeine rescues apneas, sighs, and irregular respiratory rhythms in Atoh1::En1-CKO mice, cannot be through normalizing chemoresponses and these results confirm that Atoh1-lineage rRL neurons contribute to respiratory chemoresponses to low oxygen and high carbon dioxide.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on the observation that caffeine rescues some phenotypes but not chemoresponses.

claim: Atoh1-lineage rRL neurons contribute to respiratory chemoresponses to low oxygen.
source: Thus, the mechanism by which caffeine rescues apneas, sighs, and irregular respiratory rhythms in Atoh1::En1-CKO mice, cannot be through normalizing chemoresponses and these results confirm that Atoh1-lineage rRL neurons contribute to respiratory chemoresponses to low oxygen and high carbon dioxide.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on the experimental data showing impaired hypoxic responses.

claim: Atoh1-lineage rRL neurons contribute to respiratory chemoresponses to high carbon dioxide.
source: Thus, the mechanism by which caffeine rescues apneas, sighs, and irregular respiratory rhythms in Atoh1::En1-CKO mice, cannot be through normalizing chemoresponses and these results confirm that Atoh1-lineage rRL neurons contribute to respiratory chemoresponses to low oxygen and high carbon dioxide.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on the experimental data showing attenuated hypercapnic responses.

claim: There are no previous reports that PBC neurons are intrinsically chemosensitive.
source: There are no previous reports that PBC neurons are intrinsically chemosensitive, so these neurons are likely activated by upstream neurons that are chemosensitive.
evidence: This is stated as a knowledge claim about the literature.

claim: Atoh1-lineage PBC neurons are likely activated by upstream neurons that are chemosensitive.
source: There are no previous reports that PBC neurons are intrinsically chemosensitive, so these neurons are likely activated by upstream neurons that are chemosensitive.
evidence: This is stated as an inference based on the lack of evidence for intrinsic chemosensitivity.

claim: Pcp2Cre/+;Slc32a1Flox/Flox mice have no defects in cell types other than Purkinje cells.
source: These Pcp2Cre/+;Slc32a1Flox/Flox mice have no defects in cell types other than PCs, and loss of PC signaling results in abnormal motor control including ataxia and poor performance on the rotarod (White et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by citation to White et al., 2014.

claim: Previous studies suggested a role for intertrigeminal neurons in the attenuation of sleep and reflex apneas.

claim: The respiratory phenotype of Atoh1::Phox2b-CKO mice results from abnormal RTN development.

claim: There are two Atoh1-lineage nuclei that rely on Atoh1 expression for their function in respiratory chemoreflexes: the PBC and RTN.

claim: Removal of Atoh1 from both PBC and RTN recapitulated the fully penetrant neonatal lethality of Atoh1-null mice.
source: Removal of Atoh1 from both of these nuclei recapitulated the fully penetrant neonatal lethality of Atoh1-null mice, which we hypothesize is caused by combined loss of CO2-evoked glutamatergic signaling (RTN) and hypoxia-induced activation of PBC neurons.

claim: Arterial CO2 unloading removes respiratory drive and results in sustained apnea in neonatal models.
source: Previous studies in neonatal models have shown that arterial CO2 unloading removes respiratory drive and results in sustained apnea, in accordance with the notion that CO2 sensing is essential for neonatal breathing (Nattie, 1999; Praud et al., 1997).

claim: CO2 sensing is essential for neonatal breathing.
source: Previous studies in neonatal models have shown that arterial CO2 unloading removes respiratory drive and results in sustained apnea, in accordance with the notion that CO2 sensing is essential for neonatal breathing (Nattie, 1999; Praud et al., 1997).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by citations.

claim: When directly or indirectly activated during respiratory chemochallenges, Atoh1-lineage neurons increase glutamatergic input to the preBötzinger complex.

claim: The preBötzinger complex is thought to form the central respiratory pattern generator.
source: We suspect that, when directly or indirectly activated during respiratory chemochallenges, Atoh1-lineage neurons increase glutamatergic input to the preBötzinger complex, which is thought to form the central respiratory pattern generator.

claim: The two pathways of chemosensation (PBC and RTN-mediated) are likely partially redundant.
source: Since neither Atoh1::En1-CKO mice nor Atoh1::Phox2b-CKO mice show complete lethality nor complete loss of respiratory chemoresponses, it is likely that these two pathways of chemosensation (PBC and RTN-mediated) are partially redundant, as would make sense for any circuit that controls a process as fundamental to survival as breathing.
evidence: This is stated as an inference in the discussion based on the partial phenotypes of single conditional knockouts.

claim: Slow respiratory frequency in Atoh1-null mice can be fully restored by application of a glutamate reuptake inhibitor.
source: Indeed, en bloc recordings from Atoh1-null mice reveal that slow respiratory frequency can be fully restored by application of a glutamate reuptake inhibitor and partially restored by substance P application (Rose et al., 2009b).

claim: Slow respiratory frequency in Atoh1-null mice can be partially restored by substance P application.
source: Indeed, en bloc recordings from Atoh1-null mice reveal that slow respiratory frequency can be fully restored by application of a glutamate reuptake inhibitor and partially restored by substance P application (Rose et al., 2009b).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by citation to Rose et al., 2009b.

evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by citations.
